stem: Every API handler your team writes is supposed to wrap backend calls in a Result type. Code Claude generates for the four engineers who started the project follows the convention. A developer who joined last week gets plain try/catch blocks from Claude on the same files. All four original engineers added the convention to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md when the project began. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Move the convention into the project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repository so every clone loads it.
Send the new developer the text and have them paste it into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
Create a .claude/skills/error-handling skill in the repository describing the Result convention.
Add the convention to the pull request template so reviewers catch handlers that do not follow it.

explanation: User-level configuration lives on one machine and is never distributed through version control. A standard the whole team must follow belongs at project level, where cloning the repository is enough to receive it.

why.B: Fixes exactly one person and has to be repeated for every future hire, which is the same failure again.
why.C: A skill loads on demand rather than always, so a universal standard would apply only when something invokes it.
why.D: Shifts the burden onto human reviewers instead of giving Claude the standard before the code is written.

stem: Two engineers run the same prompt in the same repository and get different results: one gets structured logging with correlation IDs, the other gets bare console calls. Both insist their setup is identical. Before editing any file, what is the fastest way to establish which instruction files each session actually loaded?

options.text: Add a distinctive marker sentence to the project CLAUDE.md and see whether both sessions repeat it.
Ask both engineers to paste their ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files side by side for comparison.
Have both engineers run git status and diff their working trees to find the configuration difference.
Run /memory in each session to list the loaded memory files and where each came from.

explanation: /memory exists precisely to show which memory files are in effect for the current session, across user, project and directory level, which is what makes inconsistent behaviour between sessions diagnosable.

why.A: An indirect probe that takes a round trip per guess and still does not enumerate what is loaded.
why.B: Covers only one level of the hierarchy and misses directory-level CLAUDE.md files and .claude/rules/ entirely.
why.C: Version control cannot show user-level files, which are outside the repository and are the most likely difference.

stem: Your monorepo has one root CLAUDE.md of 1,900 lines covering standards for six packages. Engineers working in packages/billing report Claude applying the GraphQL naming conventions that belong to packages/gateway, and the file is now a merge conflict hotspot on almost every release. Each package has a maintainer who owns its standards. What is the most maintainable restructuring?

options.text: Create one skill per package containing that package's standards, and invoke the right one at the start of each session.
Keep the single root file but add a clear header per package and rely on Claude to select the relevant section.
Have each package maintainer keep that package's standards in their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
Keep a short root CLAUDE.md of universal standards and give each package a CLAUDE.md that @imports only what it needs.

explanation: @import is the documented way to keep CLAUDE.md modular: each package's file references only the standards files relevant to it, so irrelevant conventions never load and each maintainer edits a separate file.

why.A: Turns always-relevant standards into something that loads only when someone remembers to invoke it.
why.B: Relies on the model inferring which header applies, which is exactly the inference that is already failing in packages/billing.
why.C: User-level files are private to one machine, so the standards would stop reaching anyone else on the team.

stem: Your project CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines covering testing, API conventions, deployment and logging. Any pull request that adjusts a convention conflicts in that one file, and reviewers cannot tell from the diff which topic changed. The conventions genuinely need to be in effect for the whole project. What structure best addresses this?

options.text: Split the content into topic-specific files under .claude/rules/, such as testing.md, api-conventions.md and logging.md.
Split the content into subdirectory CLAUDE.md files placed near the code that each topic concerns, so every convention sits beside the code it governs.
Move the less frequently edited half into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to shrink the committed file.
Keep the single file and add a table of contents plus section anchors at the top.

explanation: .claude/rules/ is the documented alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md: topic files stay project-wide and version-controlled, but each topic has its own file to edit, review and own.

why.B: Directory-level files apply to work in that tree, and deployment or logging conventions are not confined to one directory.
why.C: User-level files are not shared, so half the team standards would silently vanish for everyone else.
why.D: Cosmetic: one file still means one merge conflict surface and one opaque diff.

stem: Your team is documenting how Claude Code configuration reaches each engineer. Which two statements about the CLAUDE.md hierarchy are correct? (Select 2)

options.text: Because user-level configuration is read first, placing a convention in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is the most reliable way to make it apply to everyone on the project.
Instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md apply only to that user's own sessions and are not distributed through version control.
A subdirectory CLAUDE.md applies to work in that directory tree, which makes it a poor fit for conventions whose files are scattered across the repository.
Splitting a CLAUDE.md into .claude/rules/ files changes when the content loads, because rules files are only read after an explicit /memory call.

explanation: The hierarchy is user, project and directory. User-level is private to one machine, and directory-level is bound to its directory tree, which is why glob-scoped rules exist for conventions that follow a file type rather than a location.

why.A: Reverses the point: user-level configuration is the one place a convention cannot reach teammates from.
why.D: Invented mechanism. /memory reports which memory files are loaded, it does not trigger loading.

stem: You like Claude to run the linter after every edit and to write unusually verbose commit messages. You committed both preferences to the repository's root CLAUDE.md, and a teammate has opened a pull request objecting that these are personal habits now imposed on twelve people's sessions. They are right. Where does this instruction belong?

options.text: In a project skill under .claude/skills/ that only you invoke.
In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies to your sessions on your machine and is not distributed to teammates.
In the root CLAUDE.md but wrapped in a section clearly headed "optional personal preferences" that teammates are free to ignore.
In a .claude/rules/ file with a paths pattern covering the whole repository.

explanation: The user level exists for exactly this: preferences that should shape your own sessions and no one else's. Nothing personal needs to enter version control to take effect.

why.A: A project skill is version-controlled and shared, and it also needs invoking, which a working preference should not.
why.C: Still loaded in every teammate's session; a header asking the model to treat instructions as optional is not scoping.
why.D: A rules file is still committed, so the preference still reaches every teammate whose work matches the pattern.

stem: Your packages/payments/CLAUDE.md contains the import line @../../docs/pci-standards.md, and the PCI rules are applied correctly in your sessions. A contractor reports Claude never applies them. Running /memory in the contractor's session lists packages/payments/CLAUDE.md but nothing for the imported file. In the contractor's clone, git ls-files shows no entry for docs/pci-standards.md and a .gitignore rule matches that path. What is the correct diagnosis and fix?

options.text: The import target is gitignored, so the contractor's clone has no such file; track and commit it.
Replace the @import with a committed skill under .claude/skills/ that carries the PCI standards.
@import can only reference files under .claude/, so the standards file must be moved there to be resolvable.
The contractor should paste the PCI rules into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so the rules are present locally.

explanation: @import inlines a file from the checkout. If the target is not committed, teammates clone the importing file but not its target, which is exactly what /memory shows here.

why.B: A skill would be committed, but it also converts always-on standards into on-demand ones, and it does not explain the missing file.
why.C: Invented restriction; the import path is not the problem, the missing file is.
why.D: A per-person workaround that must be repeated for everyone and drifts from the canonical standards.

stem: You built a /scratch command that prints your personal debugging preamble and opens your own notes file. You committed it to the repository's .claude/commands/ directory two months ago. It now appears in every teammate's slash menu, three of them have run it by mistake, and one has filed a bug asking what the notes file is. Where does the command belong?

options.text: In ~/.claude/commands/, which is personal and applies to your sessions in any repository.
In .claude/commands/ with a leading underscore in the filename, which hides it from the slash menu.
In .claude/commands/ with a description line telling teammates the command is for one person's use.
In your ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md as an instruction block describing the same preamble and notes file.

explanation: User-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/ are personal and are never distributed with the repository, so /scratch stops appearing in anyone else's slash menu while still working in every session of yours.

why.B: Invented convention. A filename prefix does not remove a committed command from the repository or from the menu.
why.C: The file is still committed and still listed for everyone; a note in the description is documentation, not scoping.
why.D: CLAUDE.md carries context rather than command definitions, so the invocation is lost and the preamble loads in every session instead of on demand.

stem: Your team's /audit-deps skill walks the dependency tree, which puts roughly 40,000 tokens of transitive dependency listings into the transcript as tool results before the skill summarises four risky packages. Engineers report that after running it mid-task, the session has lost the thread of the feature they were implementing and starts asking about files it had already read. What is the smallest change that fixes this?

options.text: Instruct the skill body to report only the four risky packages and to suppress the full dependency listings.
Have engineers run /compact immediately after each invocation so the listings are summarised away.
Add context: fork to the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter so it runs in an isolated context and returns only its summary.
Set allowed-tools in the frontmatter to Read and Grep so the skill works through fewer tools while it walks the tree.

explanation: context: fork exists for skills whose output is verbose or exploratory: the work happens in an isolated sub-agent context and only the result returns, so the main conversation keeps the feature work intact.

why.A: A prompt-level request for less output when the volume arrives as tool results, before any summary is written.
why.B: Reactive and lossy: the context is already spent, and compaction discards the feature work along with the listings.
why.D: Restricting tools changes what the skill may do, not how much of its output reaches the conversation.

stem: A project skill that applies codemods across the repository has twice this month also run git checkout -- and rm through Bash while "tidying up", destroying uncommitted work on two engineers' machines. The skill legitimately needs to read files and write its rewrites. What is the appropriate configuration change?

options.text: Move the skill to ~/.claude/skills/ so only its author, who knows what it does, can run it.
Add a line to the skill body forbidding git checkout, rm and any other destructive shell command.
Set allowed-tools in the frontmatter to the read and edit tools it needs, leaving out Bash.
Add context: fork so the codemod runs in an isolated sub-agent context, away from the main session.

explanation: allowed-tools restricts which tools are available while the skill runs, which is a deterministic guarantee. If Bash is not available, the destructive command cannot be issued at all.

why.A: Changes who can run it, not what it can do, and the author's uncommitted work is still at risk.
why.B: A prompt instruction where an enforceable restriction exists; compliance stays probabilistic and the cost of a miss is lost work.
why.D: fork isolates conversation context, not filesystem effects, so the same rm would still delete the same files.

stem: Your /new-endpoint skill needs a resource name and an HTTP method to scaffold correctly. Developers invoke it as a bare /new-endpoint about 70% of the time, after which the skill either stops to ask a follow-up question or guesses and produces scaffolding that has to be deleted. Which frontmatter field addresses this directly?

options.text: allowed-tools, which lists exactly the tools the skill is permitted to use while it scaffolds a new endpoint.
context: fork, so scaffolding built on a wrong guess stays inside the sub-agent context.
argument-hint, which prompts for the parameters the skill expects when it is invoked bare.
The description field, rewritten to name the resource and the HTTP method the skill needs.

explanation: argument-hint is the frontmatter field for exactly this: it tells the developer which parameters the skill needs at the moment they invoke it without them.

why.A: Restricts tool access; it says nothing about missing input.
why.B: Isolates output, so the wrong scaffolding is still generated and still has to be redone.
why.D: description governs when a skill is selected, not what the developer is asked for at invocation time.

stem: Your team's naming and error-handling standards are meant to apply to every line of code Claude writes, in every session, with nobody having to remember anything. A colleague has put them in .claude/skills/coding-standards/SKILL.md. Reviewers are still catching code that ignores the standards several times a week. What is the correct placement?

options.text: Keep the skill and add a CLAUDE.md line instructing Claude to invoke the coding-standards skill at the start of every session.
Move the standards into the project CLAUDE.md, which loads automatically in every session.
Move the skill to ~/.claude/skills/ for each engineer so it is closer to their session.
Keep the skill and add context: fork so its standards do not compete with the task in the main context.

explanation: Skills are for on-demand, task-specific workflows; CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded universal standards. Standards that must apply everywhere should not depend on something choosing to invoke them.

why.A: Adds indirection while keeping activation probabilistic, when the content could simply be in the always-loaded file.
why.C: User-scoped and still on demand, so it is both unshared and unreliable.
why.D: fork isolates a skill's output; it does nothing to make the skill load automatically.

stem: Your project CLAUDE.md contains a 600-line section describing the ten-step release-note generation procedure, which the team runs about twice a month. Engineers complain that ordinary sessions now open with a large block of instructions irrelevant to the work in front of them. Where should the procedure live?

options.text: In the same CLAUDE.md, moved to the bottom of the file below the day-to-day standards.
In a .claude/rules/release-notes.md topic file with no paths frontmatter, keeping it out of CLAUDE.md.
In a CLAUDE.md placed in the docs/ subdirectory where release notes are written.
In a skill under .claude/skills/, invoked on demand when release notes are actually being produced.

explanation: An occasional, task-specific procedure is what skills are for. CLAUDE.md should hold the universal standards that every session genuinely needs.

why.A: Position in the file does not change the fact that all 600 lines load every time.
why.B: A rules file with no paths field loads at launch for the whole project, so all 600 lines are still in every session.
why.C: Release notes draw on the whole repository, and the content would still load for every session that touches docs/.

stem: Your repository ships a shared skill at .claude/skills/review-checklist/SKILL.md. You want a stricter personal version for your own sessions, with extra security checks, without changing what teammates get. Which two actions are correct? (Select 2)

options.text: Create the variant under ~/.claude/skills/, which is personal and not distributed through version control.
Add context: fork to the shared skill so your stricter checks apply only inside your own context.
Edit .claude/skills/review-checklist/SKILL.md in place and remember not to commit the change.
Give the personal variant a different name so it does not collide with or shadow the team's skill.

explanation: Personal customisation belongs in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name. That keeps the shared skill untouched for the team and avoids any ambiguity about which skill an invocation resolves to.

why.B: fork controls context isolation, not who a skill applies to, so teammates would still get your version.
why.C: An uncommitted edit to a tracked team file shows up in every diff and eventually gets committed by accident.

stem: A shared skill reads the payments service and collects the request and response shape of all 40 endpoints, so the session can then rewrite the client against them. A teammate added context: fork to its SKILL.md last week. Since then the main session receives a four-line summary naming the endpoint groups, and the rewrite that follows re-reads the same files the skill already read. What is the correct change?

options.text: Remove context: fork from the frontmatter, because the main session needs the shapes the skill collects.
Keep context: fork and have the skill write the shapes to a scratch file that the main session reads afterwards.
Keep context: fork and ask the skill for a longer summary listing every field of every endpoint.
Move the skill to ~/.claude/skills/ so it runs under the invoking engineer's own configuration.

explanation: context: fork is for skills whose detail should stay out of the main conversation. Here the detail is the deliverable the next step consumes, so isolating it removes exactly what the work needs.

why.B: Adds a file-passing protocol to work around one line of frontmatter that should not be there.
why.C: A summary that carries every field of every endpoint is the full output again, with no guarantee it is returned.
why.D: Scope decides who can run a skill, not where its output lands, so the main session still receives only the summary.

stem: Your monorepo keeps infrastructure code in two places: a top-level terraform/ tree and per-service services/*/infra/ directories. The 400-line Terraform convention set, covering required tags, module structure and remote state layout, must apply to every .tf file wherever it lives, and must not load during ordinary application work. What is the correct configuration?

options.text: Append the conventions to the root CLAUDE.md under a Terraform header so they are always available.
A .claude/skills/terraform-conventions skill that engineers invoke whenever infrastructure work begins.
Put a CLAUDE.md in terraform/ and a copy in each services/*/infra/ directory, beside the code it governs.
A .claude/rules/terraform.md file with frontmatter paths: ["**/*.tf"].

explanation: A glob in the paths frontmatter follows the file type rather than a location, so one rule file covers both trees and loads only when a .tf file is in play, keeping the 400 lines out of application sessions.

why.A: Loads all 400 lines in every session, which is the cost being avoided, and leaves applicability to inference.
why.B: Requires someone or something to invoke it, when the requirement is automatic activation based on the file path.
why.C: Duplicates the conventions across directories, and a new copy must be added by hand for every new service.

stem: You packaged your controller conventions as a skill so they would load "only when needed". An audit over two weeks shows the conventions were applied in 61% of the controller files Claude generated or edited; in the rest, the skill was simply never invoked. The files needing the conventions are identifiable purely by name: **/*.controller.ts. What is the right change?

options.text: Move the conventions into the root CLAUDE.md so they are always loaded and cannot be missed.
Move the conventions into a .claude/rules/ file with paths: ["**/*.controller.ts"].
Rewrite the skill's description so Claude recognises more of the situations that should invoke it.
Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md instructing Claude to invoke the conventions skill before it edits or creates any controller file.

explanation: When the trigger is a file path, path-scoped rules make activation deterministic: the rule loads because the file matches, not because the model decided to fetch it.

why.A: Would apply the conventions, but loads 100% of them in the majority of sessions that never touch a controller.
why.C: Improves the invocation rate but keeps it probabilistic, when deterministic path matching is available.
why.D: Still depends on the model following an instruction on every edit, so the 39% gap only narrows.

stem: Database migrations live inside each service: services/billing/db/migrations/, services/catalog/db/migrations/, and eleven more like them. Every migration must follow the same reversible-migration convention, and the platform team adds roughly one new service a month. Which approach needs the least maintenance as services are added?

options.text: One .claude/rules/migrations.md with frontmatter paths: ["services/*/db/migrations/**"].
A CLAUDE.md inside each service's db/migrations/ directory, added to the service template so new services get one.
A Migrations section in the root CLAUDE.md that describes the convention for all services.
A PostToolUse hook that inspects every written migration file and flags the ones with no down step.

explanation: A single glob covers the thirteen existing directories and every future one automatically, and it loads only while migration files are being worked on.

why.B: Thirteen copies today and one more per service, which drift as the convention evolves.
why.C: Loads for every session regardless of the work, and leaves it to inference whether the section applies.
why.D: Builds enforcement machinery to catch mistakes after the file is written instead of supplying the convention beforehand.

stem: A teammate is unsure when a .claude/rules/ file with a paths frontmatter field is the right tool. Which two statements about path-scoped rules are correct? (Select 2)

options.text: A paths field can only name directories, so conventions tied to a file type such as **/*.test.tsx must use a directory-level CLAUDE.md instead.
A path-scoped rule replaces the project CLAUDE.md while a matching file is open, so any shared standards must be repeated inside each rule file.
They activate according to whether the file being worked on matches the glob, rather than according to a decision by the model to load them.
They keep conventions out of context while non-matching files are being worked on, reducing irrelevant context and token usage.

explanation: Path-scoped rules give deterministic activation by file path and conditional loading, which is what makes them both more reliable than skills and cheaper than a monolithic always-loaded file.

why.A: Reverses the actual advantage: glob patterns are precisely how conventions follow a file type across directories.
why.B: Invented behaviour; rules supplement the loaded configuration rather than replacing it.

stem: You added .claude/rules/testing.md with paths: ["tests/**/*"] to enforce the team's test conventions. Compliance in the integration suite under tests/ is now good, but roughly 300 colocated unit tests written next to their sources, such as src/checkout/Cart.test.ts, still ignore the conventions entirely. What is the smallest correct fix?

options.text: Move the 300 colocated tests into tests/ so the existing rule matches them with no pattern change.
Widen the glob to match by file type wherever tests live: paths: ["**/*.test.ts", "tests/**/*"].
Move the test conventions from the rules file into the root CLAUDE.md so they are always in context.
Add a CLAUDE.md carrying the same conventions to each src subdirectory that holds colocated tests.

explanation: The rule mechanism is already right; only the pattern is too narrow. A type-based glob follows the test files across every directory they live in, which is the reason glob rules beat directory-bound configuration here.

why.A: Restructures the codebase to suit the tooling, which is a large change for a one-line pattern problem.
why.C: Loads test conventions in every session, including work that never touches a test, and returns applicability to inference.
why.D: Directory-bound duplication across dozens of directories, which drifts and must be extended for every new module.

stem: A production stack trace names one line: parseExpiry in src/billing/card.ts throws on card expiry values in the form 2/2027 because the regex requires two digits for the month. The fix is one conditional in one function. A teammate suggests entering plan mode first because it is a payments bug. What is the appropriate approach?

options.text: Delegate to the Explore subagent to map how the billing module parses card fields first.
Direct execution: one function, a cause the stack trace already names, and one obvious fix.
Plan mode, because any change to payment code should be planned in writing before it is made.
Plan mode, so that every other regex in the billing module that might share the same two-digit month weakness is enumerated first.

explanation: Plan mode earns its cost when scope is large, the approach is undecided, or the code has to be explored first. None of that is true when a stack trace has already localised a one-line fix.

why.A: Discovery isolation for a problem that is already located precisely.
why.C: Treats plan mode as a risk ritual rather than a tool for undecided or wide-ranging work, adding overhead with nothing to explore.
why.D: Expands the task beyond the reported defect, which is a separate piece of work and a separate decision.

stem: You must migrate 47 files from a deprecated HTTP client to its replacement. Two call sites use streaming semantics the new client models differently, and the team has not yet decided whether to hide the new client behind an adapter or change every call site directly. Which approach fits?

options.text: Direct execution file by file, deciding the adapter question when you reach the two streaming call sites.
Stay in plan mode through the whole migration so every one of the 47 edits is reviewed as part of the plan.
Plan mode to survey the call sites and settle the adapter question, then direct execution to carry out the agreed plan.
Direct execution driven by an exhaustive upfront instruction specifying how each of the 47 files should change.

explanation: Plan mode covers the part that is genuinely uncertain, the architectural choice and its blast radius, and direct execution covers the mechanical edits once the choice is made. Combining the two is the documented pattern for a migration of this shape.

why.A: Defers an architectural decision until 45 files are already committed to one shape, which is how costly rework happens.
why.B: Keeps a design tool in place for work that is fully understood once the decision is made, slowing the mechanical majority.
why.D: You cannot specify how 47 files should change before examining how they use the client, which is the exploration being skipped.

stem: A four-phase task begins with "find every place session tokens are created, validated or revoked" across a 900-file service. Run directly, the grep output and file reads filled most of the context window during phase one, and by phase three the session had lost the findings from phase one and started re-reading the same files. How should the work be structured?

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window so all four phases and their search output fit.
Run the discovery phase through the Explore subagent, so only its summary returns to the main conversation.
Split the four phases across four separate sessions, with the engineer pasting the findings forward by hand.
Run /compact after the discovery phase to reclaim the context the searches consumed before phase two.

explanation: The Explore subagent exists for verbose discovery: the searching happens in an isolated context and the main conversation receives the summary, so later phases still have the findings and the room to use them.

why.A: A bigger window postpones the same exhaustion without changing what enters the conversation.
why.C: Shifts the work onto the engineer and reintroduces exactly the handoff losses being reported.
why.D: Acts after the context is already spent, and compaction decides what to keep, so phase-one findings may still be lost.

stem: The product needs full-text search. Three implementations are viable: Postgres tsvector columns, an external search service, or an in-process index. They differ in operational cost and two of them require infrastructure the team does not run today. No decision has been made and nobody has looked at how the current query layer is structured. Which approach fits?

options.text: Begin in direct execution and switch to plan mode if the chosen approach turns out to be the wrong one.
Direct execution with the Postgres option, since it is the only one that needs no new infrastructure.
Plan mode, to explore the existing query layer and compare the three approaches with their infrastructure implications.
Implement all three behind a common interface and benchmark them against production traffic.

explanation: Multiple valid approaches with different infrastructure implications, and a codebase nobody has examined, is the case plan mode is designed for. The decision is the task.

why.A: The three approaches and their infrastructure differences are already on the table, so nothing is waiting to emerge that would trigger the switch.
why.B: Picks an approach on one criterion before the comparison that was the actual work.
why.D: Builds three implementations to answer a question that exploration and comparison can answer far more cheaply.

stem: You are triaging this sprint's backlog and deciding how to approach each item with Claude Code. Which two tasks most clearly warrant plan mode rather than direct execution? (Select 2)

options.text: Splitting a utils package used by nine services into domain packages, with boundaries not yet agreed.
Renaming a configuration key in the three files that reference it, with the new name agreed and the call sites already listed.
A major web framework upgrade touching routing, data fetching and the build configuration.
Adding a null check to one function after a stack trace names the line, with the fix agreed in review.

explanation: Plan mode fits large-scale, multi-file work with architectural decisions or several valid approaches. Both the package split and the framework upgrade are undecided in shape and wide in blast radius.

why.B: Mechanical, three files, and the decision is already made, so there is nothing to plan.
why.D: A single-file fix with a known cause, which is the textbook case for direct execution.

stem: In a plan-mode session for a payments refactor, the exploration step alone produced about 60,000 tokens of directory listings and file reads. By the time the plan was written the session was near its limit, and the plan silently omitted two modules that had been read early on. Plan mode is still the right call for this work. What is the most effective adjustment?

options.text: Abandon plan mode and use direct execution, refactoring module by module as you go.
Have the exploration write its findings to a scratch file, then start a fresh session and write the plan from that file.
Delegate discovery to the Explore subagent, which isolates the verbose output and returns a summary to plan from.
Have the engineer list the relevant files by hand before the session starts so no exploration is needed.

explanation: The failure is discovery volume crowding out the plan, not planning itself. Isolating exploration in the Explore subagent preserves the main conversation for the design work that has to remember everything.

why.A: Removes the design step this refactor needs, when the problem is where the discovery output lands.
why.B: A manual handoff that drops the reasoning already built up in the session and does by hand what the Explore subagent does inside it.
why.D: Shifts the work onto the engineer and presumes the answer that the exploration exists to find.

stem: You have described the required log-line transformation in prose three times, each version more careful than the last. Each attempt produces a different interpretation of what to do with the trailing request ID and how to format durations, sometimes 1.2s and sometimes 1200ms. You have two real before and after samples on your screen. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Write a formal grammar for the source log format and provide that instead of a description.
Move to a larger model, on the view that the existing description is being read too loosely.
Write a fourth, stricter prose description that spells out the trailing request ID and the duration rules in more emphatic language.
Give two or three input and output pairs showing the request ID and duration exactly as they should appear.

explanation: Concrete input and output examples are the most effective way to communicate a transformation when prose is being read inconsistently. Two samples settle both ambiguities without another round of wording.

why.A: Specifies the input precisely and the output not at all, which is where the disagreement actually is.
why.B: Treats a specification gap as a model capability problem; the requirement is genuinely underdetermined.
why.C: Rewriting the prose a fourth time is the failure loop already in progress; emphasis does not resolve ambiguity.

stem: A date-parsing utility must handle nine input formats, three timezone edge cases and a 5 ms per-call budget. Your working method is to run it, find a case it gets wrong, report that case, and repeat. Four rounds in, each fix repairs the reported case and quietly breaks one that worked two rounds ago. What working method fits this task better?

options.text: Write the test suite first, covering expected behaviour, the edge cases and the performance budget, then share the failing tests.
Record the nine formats and three timezone rules as conventions in the project CLAUDE.md.
Continue reporting failures one at a time, but describe each one in more detail than the last.
Ask for a fresh implementation from scratch each time a case fails, so that no earlier mistake is ever carried forward into the next one.

explanation: Test-driven iteration turns each round into a full regression check: the whole suite runs, so a fix that breaks an earlier case is visible immediately rather than two rounds later.

why.B: CLAUDE.md carries standards, not verification, so nothing detects the regressions.
why.C: This is the loop that is already failing; more detail per case still leaves every other case unverified.
why.D: Discards working behaviour every round and gives no reason to expect convergence.

stem: You are adding a caching layer to a service in a domain you have never worked in. You are confident you will miss considerations: how entries are invalidated, what happens on a cold-start stampede, and how the service should behave when the cache is unreachable. You cannot list them precisely because you do not know what you do not know. Which technique best fits?

options.text: Ask for an implementation and review it carefully against a checklist of caching concerns.
Ask for three different implementations and compare them side by side to see which design considerations each one happens to cover.
Ask Claude to interview you about invalidation, failure modes and consistency before writing code.
Write a test suite for the caching behaviour first and iterate on the failures it produces.

explanation: The interview pattern exists for exactly this gap: having Claude ask questions surfaces design considerations the developer had not anticipated, before an implementation freezes the wrong assumptions.

why.A: You cannot review for considerations you have not thought of, which is the stated problem.
why.B: Produces volume rather than questions, and three implementations may share the same blind spot.
why.D: A test suite can only encode the behaviour you already anticipated, so the unanticipated cases stay untested.

stem: A generated import script has three problems: it opens a database connection per row, it mishandles null values in the optional phone column, and its error handling swallows exceptions so failures are silent. Moving to a shared connection requires restructuring the loop, the null handling sits inside that loop, and the error handling wraps it. How should you report these?

options.text: Report the connection problem alone now, and re-review the script for the other two once it is fixed.
One detailed message covering all three, with the null input row and its expected output.
Ask for the script to be rewritten from scratch, mentioning only that the previous attempt had several problems that need fixing.
Three messages in sequence, one issue each, verifying the script after every individual fix.

explanation: When fixes interact, a single detailed message lets all three be addressed in one coherent restructuring. Sequential iteration is for independent problems, where one fix cannot disturb another.

why.A: Leaves two known defects in place and pays for another discovery pass to find them again.
why.C: Throws away the working parts and communicates none of the specifics, particularly the null case.
why.D: Each fix reworks the loop the previous one just changed, so earlier work is repeatedly undone.

stem: A migration script fails on about 4% of rows. You have twice said that null values should be handled gracefully, and got two different behaviours: once the row was skipped, once an empty string was written. The actual rule is that a null middle_name must be written as NULL and a null country must default to 'US'. What is the most effective way to communicate this?

options.text: Add NOT NULL constraints to the target schema so rows with nulls are rejected at write time.
Give a worked example per field: an input row with null middle_name and null country, and the exact output row.
Restate that nulls must be handled gracefully, adding that this matters for both fields and that the behaviour must not be guessed at.
Add a rule to the project CLAUDE.md stating that null handling must always be explicit.

explanation: The word "gracefully" is the ambiguity, and the two behaviours seen are both defensible readings of it. A worked input and expected output per field states the rule without leaving anything to interpretation.

why.A: Changes the data contract to dodge specifying behaviour, and rejects rows whose nulls are legitimate.
why.C: Emphasis does not remove ambiguity; the instruction is still compatible with skipping the row.
why.D: A general standard does not carry the two per-field rules, so the same two readings remain open.

stem: Your review job runs claude -p "Review the diff and list the issues" and a shell script then parses the prose with regular expressions to place inline pull request comments. Around 15% of runs put a comment on the wrong line or drop a finding entirely, whenever the prose formatting shifts between numbered lists and prose paragraphs. What change to the invocation fixes this?

options.text: Keep the prose output but require the prompt to emit a fixed Markdown table with one row per issue.
Pipe the prose through a second claude -p call that converts it into JSON before the script parses it.
Add --output-format json with a --json-schema defining file, line, severity and message.
Set CLAUDE_OUTPUT=json in the job environment so every invocation returns JSON without touching the script.

explanation: --output-format json with --json-schema is the documented way to get machine-parseable structured findings out of a non-interactive run, which removes the prose parsing step entirely.

why.A: A prompt-level formatting request where a schema-enforced structure is available, so drift remains possible on every run.
why.B: Two model calls where one flag would do, and the second call's output is still unconstrained by any schema.
why.D: There is no CLAUDE_OUTPUT environment variable. Output format is set by the --output-format flag.

stem: Your automated review runs on every push to a pull request. One long-lived pull request now carries the same "unbounded query in getOrders" finding four times, once per push and worded slightly differently each time, and three developers have muted the bot. The finding is genuine and still unfixed. What is the correct change?

options.text: Deduplicate on the CI side by hashing the text of each finding and dropping any hash that has already been posted to the pull request.
Run the review only once, on the first push, and rely on the pre-merge check for anything added later.
Review only the diff added since the previous push rather than the whole pull request diff each time.
Include the prior findings in each re-run, with instructions to report only new or still-unaddressed ones.

explanation: Giving the review its own prior findings is what lets it distinguish new problems from ones already raised, so re-runs add information rather than repeating it.

why.A: Findings get reworded between runs, so text hashes miss the duplicates that matter while still paying for the whole review.
why.B: Leaves every commit after the first unreviewed, which is a larger loss than the duplicate comments.
why.C: An unfixed issue in an earlier commit falls out of scope entirely, and interactions between new and existing code go unreviewed.

stem: Your CI test-generation step proposes 30 to 40 tests per pull request. Reviewers report that most of them re-test scenarios the existing suite already covers, and the two or three genuinely new cases are lost in the noise. Adoption of the suggestions has fallen to near zero. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Ask reviewers to delete the duplicates before the suggestions are posted to the pull request.
Cap the step at ten suggestions per pull request so reviewers have a shorter list to work through.
Run the proposed tests against coverage tooling and drop any that do not raise line coverage.
Put the existing tests for the touched modules in context and ask only for scenarios not already covered.

explanation: The step is duplicating coverage because it cannot see the coverage. Putting the relevant existing tests in context lets it compare against what exists, which is the root cause rather than the symptom.

why.A: Moves the filtering onto humans, which is the cost the automation was meant to remove.
why.B: Arbitrary truncation is as likely to cut the two useful cases as the duplicates.
why.C: Line coverage overlap is not the same as scenario novelty, and the duplicates are generated and paid for either way.

stem: The tests your CI job generates compile and pass, but reviewers call them low value: they assert on framework behaviour, they build customer objects by hand instead of using the project's makeCustomer fixture factory, and they ignore the team rule that a test name states the behaviour under test. The job runs claude -p from a fresh checkout of the repository. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Document the testing standards and available fixtures in the project CLAUDE.md, which the CI checkout carries.
Add the standards and the fixture list to the reviewing engineers' own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files.
Ask for more tests per pull request so a larger absolute number of valuable ones appears.
Add a post-processing step that deletes any generated test which does not reference one of the project's fixture factories.

explanation: CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for giving a CI-invoked session project context. Because the job runs from a checkout, committed standards and fixture conventions load automatically and raise the quality of what is generated.

why.B: User-level files live on individual machines, and the CI runner is not one of them, so the job would still see nothing.
why.C: More output of the same quality makes the reviewers' problem worse, not better.
why.D: Filters the symptom after generation and still produces tests that assert on framework behaviour under badly chosen names.

stem: Your pipeline has one Claude Code session implement a feature and then, in that same session, review its own diff. Across 60 pull requests the self-review raised 3 issues. A separate review instance run over the same 60 diffs raised 24, of which 19 were confirmed real by the developers. Which two of the following are correct? (Select 2)

options.text: Keep the single session but prompt it to review its work a second time with stricter, more adversarial wording.
The generating session carries the assumptions that produced the code, so it is unlikely to question them.
Have the generating session re-read the changed files from disk before reviewing, so it judges the code and not its memory of writing it.
Run the review as a separate invocation with its own context, given the diff and the review criteria.

explanation: Session context isolation is the point: a fresh instance evaluates the diff on its merits, while the generating session is reasoning from the same premises that produced the code. Running the review as its own invocation is what creates that isolation.

why.A: Stricter wording does not change the shared context, which is the cause of the blind spot.
why.C: Those files are already in that session's context; re-reading them does not remove the assumptions that produced them.
